examples.knowledge_point: Completing a Truth Table for an Equivalence
examples.problem:
What are the missing entries in the following truth table?

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\, ( \neg P \land Q) \Leftrightarrow Q \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\phantom{F}}$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\phantom{F}}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\phantom{F}}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\phantom{F}}$ |
examples.worked_solution:
According to the definition of the biconditional, 

- $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A\Rightarrow B$ **and** $B\Rightarrow A.$ Otherwise, it is false.

- In other words, $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A$ and $B$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

First, we add columns for $\neg P$ and $\neg P \land Q{:}$

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\, \neg P \,$ | $\, \neg P \land Q \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |

Finally, we add a column for $(\neg P \land Q) \Leftrightarrow Q.$ 

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\, \neg P \,$ | $\, \neg P \land Q \,$ | $\, (\neg P \land Q) \Leftrightarrow Q \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |

feedback.problem: If $A$ is false and $B$ is true, then $A⇔¬B$ is{{field-1}}.
feedback.worked_solution:
According to the definition of the biconditional, 

- $P⇔Q$ is true if $P⇒Q$ **and** $Q⇒P.$ Otherwise, it is false.

- In other words, $P⇔Q$ is true if $P$ and $Q$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

So, when $A=\text{F}$ and $B=\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(A⇔¬B) & =(\text{F}⇔¬\text{T}) \\  & =(\text{F}⇔\text{F}) \\  & =\text{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

The complete truth table is shown below:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬B\,$ | $\,A⇔¬B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
|  |  |  |  |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
